chunks: "A power plane is a whole layer of the PCB that's solid copper tied to one net, like ground or 3. 3 volts.
A shape, or a pour or polygon, is the same thing but only over part of a layer, where it shares space with routing.
Either way, you're making the supply a big sheet of copper instead of a skinny wire. They're preferred because current in a sheet spreads out in two dimensions.
A trace is a resistor with a length-to-width ratio, so a 1 mm trace over 25 mm is 25 squares, about 12 milliohms for one ounce copper.
A plane spreading out from a via is more like a fraction of a milliohm because the current fans out and the resistance only grows with the log of the distance.
That means less voltage drop and less heating. It's also much lower inductance.
The plane sits right above its return plane, so the loop area is tiny, and the two planes also form a small distributed capacitor that helps decoupling at high frequency.
And you can reach it from anywhere with a via, which makes routing simpler, plus it spreads heat.

The things I watch for are splits and slots in the plane that force return current around, isolated islands, and not using a big shape on a node that switches or is sensitive, because a big copper area there is an antenna or a noise coupler."
